title: WebAssembly — The Binary Format
description: The container a compiler and a runtime agree on. Eight bytes of header, thirteen section kinds in a required order, one variable-width encoding governing almost every number in between, and the object format the core specification deliberately does not define.
author: Underlayer
completion_criteria: Read the container framing end to end, explain why each field is the width it is, and decode every declaration section of a real module by hand.

concepts.title: Why a Binary Format
concepts.description: What the format is for, and the three independent readers every claim in this course is cross-checked against.

concepts.title: The Eight-Byte Header
concepts.description: The only fixed-width integers in the framing: a magic compared byte by byte and a version read as a little-endian number.

concepts.title: Sections
concepts.description: The framing, the fourteen identifiers, the ordering rule, and a place where two reference tools report different numbers for the same custom section.

concepts.title: LEB128
concepts.description: The encoding almost every number uses, and the signed/unsigned split that gives the same two bytes three different answers.

concepts.title: The Type Section
concepts.description: Five value types, one form tag, and why a signature's identity is a position rather than a name.

concepts.title: Imports and Index Spaces
concepts.description: Per-kind import bodies, and the rule that puts imports first in all five index spaces.

concepts.title: Tables, Memories and Limits
concepts.description: One flag byte that is a length in disguise, shared by three proposals.

concepts.title: Globals and Initialisers
concepts.description: Mutability as the module's whole safety story, and an initialiser that is an expression to be walked.

concepts.title: The Code Section
concepts.description: Body framing, run-length local declarations, and why the group count is not the number of locals.

concepts.title: Instruction Encoding
concepts.description: The one-byte opcode space, the reserved top four bits, and the immediates that hide in plain sight.

concepts.title: The Element Section
concepts.description: Eight encodings for one job, the flag byte, and the elemkind byte whose only legal value is zero.

concepts.title: The Data Section and DataCount
concepts.description: Three data forms, and the four-byte section that exists only to let an earlier one be checked.

concepts.title: Objects, Linking and Relocations
concepts.description: Custom sections the core ignores, the five-byte LEB128 every real object uses, and a relocation that patches code.
